experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/title: Augustine's conversion in the Milan garden: 'Take up and read'
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/account: Confessions 8.12 (trans. E.B. Pusey, 1838, public domain): weeping under a fig tree, Augustine hears from a neighbouring house a child's voice chanting 'Take up and read; take up and read.' He opens the apostle's letters at Romans 13:13-14 and reports that 'by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away.' He was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Months later at Ostia he and his mother Monica shared a brief contemplative ascent (Confessions 9.10).
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/contemp: Augustine himself interprets the voice as a divine command, comparing it to Antony's hearing of the Gospel in church. The Confessions frame the moment as the climax of grace overcoming a divided will.
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/assessm: A classic of grace-wrought conversion valued by both Catholic and Protestant traditions; Luther and Calvin read it as a witness to the priority of grace.
Augustine is honoured as a saint in Orthodoxy but his theology is received with reservations; the conversion story is admired as a personal testimony.

Written about eleven years later (c. 397-400), the account is a carefully crafted literary-theological narrative; scholars (e.g. Pierre Courcelle) debated how literally to take the child's voice, though most accept a real crisis in the garden.
William James used Augustine as a classic case of the 'divided self' resolved in conversion.
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/debates: How much of the Confessions is literary construction?
Grace and free will: Augustine's conversion as a template for his later anti-Pelagian theology.
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/story:
Aurelius Augustinus was born in 354 at Thagaste in Roman North Africa (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria) to a pagan father, Patricius, and a devout Christian mother, Monica. Educated in rhetoric at Madaura and Carthage, he had a brilliant career as a teacher. At nineteen, reading Cicero's now lost Hortensius, he was fired with a love of wisdom; for about nine years he was a 'hearer' among the Manichaeans, who taught a dualism of light and darkness. He lived with a woman whose name he never gives, and they had a son, Adeodatus. In 384 he obtained the prestigious post of official rhetor in Milan, then an imperial residence.

His Confessions, written around 397-400 as a long prayer addressed to God, are the main source for what followed. In Milan he began to listen to the sermons of Bishop Ambrose, at first for their style, and found that Ambrose's allegorical reading of the Old Testament answered some Manichaean objections. Reading 'books of the Platonists' (probably Plotinus and Porphyry in Latin translation) helped him conceive of God as immaterial and of evil as a lack of good rather than a substance. Yet, as he describes it, he remained bound by ambition and especially by sexual desire. Monica arranged a socially suitable marriage, and his long-term partner was sent back to Africa; he took another mistress while waiting.

In Book 8 Augustine tells of the summer of 386. The elderly priest Simplicianus told him how the famous Roman rhetor Marius Victorinus had publicly professed Christianity. Then a visitor from Africa, Ponticianus, an official at the court, noticed a copy of Paul's letters on Augustine's table and told him and his friend Alypius about Antony of Egypt and about two court officials at Trier who had abandoned their careers after reading the Life of Antony. Augustine describes himself as shaken and ashamed: unlearned people were seizing heaven while he and his learning wallowed in flesh and blood.

He went out into the garden of the house where they were staying, followed by Alypius. There, he writes, he struggled with himself, his old desires seeming to pluck at his garment of flesh, while the figure of Continence invited him to trust God. He threw himself down under a fig tree and wept, asking how long it would be "tomorrow, and tomorrow". Then he heard from a neighbouring house a voice, like that of a boy or girl, repeating in a sing-song way, "Tolle lege, tolle lege", "Take up and read, take up and read." He could not remember any children's game with such words. Recalling that Antony had been converted by a Gospel reading heard as addressed to him, he went back, picked up the book of Paul's letters and read the first passage his eyes fell on: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof" (Romans 13:13-14, KJV). He writes that at once, as if a light of peace had flooded his heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished.

Alypius read the following verse, 'Him that is weak in the faith receive ye', applied it to himself and joined Augustine's resolution. They went in and told Monica, who rejoiced. Augustine resigned his teaching post at the end of the term, citing chest problems, and retired with friends and family to a country estate at Cassiciacum, where he wrote philosophical dialogues. At the Easter Vigil of 387 he, Alypius and Adeodatus were baptised by Ambrose in Milan. Shortly afterwards, at Ostia, waiting to sail for Africa, he and Monica shared a contemplative experience he describes in Book 9; she died there days later.

Back in Africa, Augustine founded a small community at Thagaste, was ordained priest at Hippo Regius in 391, almost against his will, and became its bishop around 395-396, serving until his death in 430. Historians have debated how literally to take the garden scene. In 1950 Pierre Courcelle argued that elements such as the fig tree and the voice are literary and symbolic; others note that the earlier dialogues from Cassiciacum present his conversion more as a turn to philosophy. Most accept that a decisive crisis happened in Milan in 386, while recognising that the Confessions shape it, years later, into a theological narrative of grace.
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/keyMome: Augustine is born at Thagaste in North Africa to Patricius and Monica.

Augustine is ordained priest at Hippo Regius, becoming its bishop around 395-396.
He begins writing the Confessions, which tell the story of his conversion as a prayer to God.
experiences/augustine-tolle-lege/signifi: Augustine's conversion, through the Confessions, became the classic Western account of the restless heart finding rest in God and of grace overcoming a divided will. It shaped Augustine's later theology of sin, grace and predestination, which in turn deeply influenced medieval Catholic thought, Luther, Calvin and the Jansenists. The Confessions also founded the genre of spiritual autobiography and influenced Western ideas of the self and inner life. Eastern Orthodox theologians have often been more reserved about Augustine's views on original sin and grace, and modern scholars debate how far the garden scene is shaped by literary convention, but its influence on Christian and secular culture remains enormous.
experiences/symeon-divine-light/title: Symeon the New Theologian's visions of divine light
experiences/symeon-divine-light/account: Paraphrase of Symeon's Catechetical Discourses (esp. 22), where he describes himself in the third person as a young man named George: praying at night, he is suddenly flooded with a divine light that fills the room; he loses awareness of the walls and of himself, and is filled with tears and joy. In his Hymns of Divine Love he speaks repeatedly of seeing Christ as light and insists that those who say no one can now experience God consciously deny the gospel.
experiences/symeon-divine-light/contempo: Symeon's claims and his veneration of his own spiritual father caused conflict with church authorities; he was exiled from Constantinople c. 1009 but later rehabilitated. Orthodoxy came to call him 'New Theologian', one of only three so titled (with John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus).
experiences/symeon-divine-light/assessme: A canonical teacher of the conscious experience of grace; his insistence that the Spirit's indwelling is felt, not just believed, anticipates hesychasm.
Respected as an Eastern mystic; Catholic theology generally distinguishes such experience from the created grace it posits, a difference sharpened later in the Palamite debate.

Some charismatic writers point to Symeon's 'baptism in the Spirit' language (tears, experiential certainty) as an Eastern parallel to Spirit baptism, while Orthodox scholars caution against equating the two.
His conflict with Stephen of Nicomedia illustrates the perennial tension between charismatic authority and ecclesiastical office in Byzantium.
experiences/symeon-divine-light/debates/: Charism vs. office: can an unordained or junior monk bind or loose by spiritual authority?
Is conscious experience of grace normal for all Christians?
experiences/symeon-divine-light/story:
In the tenth century Constantinople was the capital of a revived Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty, and its church was confident, wealthy and highly organised. Monasteries such as the Stoudios monastery were centres of liturgy and learning. Some critics felt that spiritual life had become routine: many assumed that the vivid experience of the Holy Spirit known to the early saints belonged to the past. The monk later called Symeon the New Theologian challenged that assumption with his own experience.

Symeon was born in 949 in Paphlagonia, in northern Asia Minor, to a family of provincial nobility, and was baptised George. As a boy he was sent to Constantinople for education and entered a career at the imperial court. At around fourteen he came under the influence of an elderly monk of Stoudios, Symeon the Studite (also called Eulabes, 'the Pious'), who became his spiritual father. The younger man continued in public life but followed a rule of prayer and reading his elder gave him, including the works of Mark the Hermit.

In his Catechetical Discourses (especially Discourse 22) Symeon describes, in the third person, the experience of a young man named George, generally accepted as himself, when he was about twenty. One evening while praying, he wrote, a divine light suddenly shone down from above and filled the room. The young man lost awareness of where he was and seemed to himself to be all light, filled with tears and joy. In the light he saw what seemed like a cloud, and next to it his spiritual father. The experience faded, and George, by his own account, fell back into a careless life for some years.

Around 977 he entered Stoudios as a novice, taking the name Symeon, but tension arose over his intense devotion to his elder, and he moved to the small monastery of St Mamas in the capital. He was ordained priest and around 980 became its abbot, serving for about twenty-five years. In his Hymns of Divine Love and his discourses he described repeated experiences of the uncreated light, which he identified with God himself, and insisted that anyone who had not consciously experienced the Holy Spirit was not yet fully a Christian. He spoke frankly of tears, of seeing Christ as light and of a personal relationship with God, in language that many found startling.

His teaching provoked resistance. Some monks at St Mamas rebelled against his demanding regime. More seriously, he clashed with Stephen, former metropolitan of Nicomedia and a learned official of the patriarchate, partly over Symeon's public veneration of his spiritual father, Symeon the Studite, as a saint, with an icon and feast, without official approval. Symeon also argued that spiritual authority, including the power to hear confessions and bind and loose, belonged to those who had experienced the Spirit, not only to the ordained. In 1009 he was exiled across the Bosphorus, where he settled at a ruined chapel of St Marina near Paloukiton and formed a new community. He was later rehabilitated but chose to stay, dying there in 1022.

His disciple Niketas Stethatos wrote his Life and edited his works. Symeon's emphasis on conscious experience of divine light was later taken up by the hesychast monks of Mount Athos, and his works were included in part in the Philokalia. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church, which gives the title 'Theologian' to only two others: John the Evangelist and Gregory of Nazianzus.
experiences/symeon-divine-light/keyMomen: Symeon, baptised George, is born in Paphlagonia to a provincial noble family.

experiences/symeon-divine-light/signific: Symeon is a pivotal figure in Byzantine mysticism, insisting that conscious experience of God as light is available and essential to Christian life, not merely a memory of the apostolic age. His ideas helped prepare the hesychast tradition and Gregory Palamas' theology of the uncreated light, and he remains central to Orthodox spirituality through the Philokalia. His claim that spiritual authority rests on experience of the Spirit raised lasting questions about charisma and church office, questions that also interest Protestant, Pentecostal and charismatic readers who see in him an Eastern witness to Spirit-filled experience. Critics, then and now, have warned that his approach could undermine ecclesial order or encourage subjective claims.
